identified_problem: Supervised assessment is rated Weak on authenticity, because timed, AI-free conditions are unlike professional computing practice and a retreat to invigilated exams may narrow what is assessed [R01], [R57], [R88], [R24]. It is also rated Weak on appropriate AI use, because it usually sits at the No-AI level and cannot develop responsible GenAI use on its own [R10], [R19]. It is only Moderate on process visibility, scalability, workload and equity, since standard exams show only the product, invigilation and live supervision take substantial staff time, and stress, accommodation and technical-failure risks rise [R84], [R95], [R51], [R25].
recommended_redesign: Use supervision as a targeted checkpoint at key programme points, such as gatekeeping or stage-gate assessments, rather than supervising every task [R68], [R04], [S097].
Make the supervised task hands-on where possible: live checkoffs in real developer tools with scripted questions and a standard rubric, instead of only pen-and-paper exams [R95].
Include supervised items that ask students to find and correct errors in AI-generated code, and give students practice with this task type before it is used for high stakes [R33].

Pair each supervised checkpoint with AI-permitted coursework in the same course, and plan accommodations, quieter spaces and fallbacks for technical failure in advance [S115], [R93], [R95], [S009], [R25].
justification: Finding: supervised performance exposed large gaps behind take-home marks, for example viva and live-demo averages of about 35% and 44% against 83.8% on take-home work [R81], and 94.8% on AI-permitted assignments against 86.3% on proctored exams [D24]. Finding: live checkoffs in real tools ran with 237 students and most respondents said they improved their skills [R95], and invigilated tasks correcting LLM code exposed debugging gaps [R33]. Interpretation: supervision gives the most direct evidence of unaided capability, so it is worth keeping, but its authenticity and AI-use weaknesses suggest it should be a targeted, hands-on component combined with AI-permitted work rather than the whole assessment [R68], [S115].
implementation_considerations: Cohort: paper or existing invigilated exams suit small cohorts with little change [R82]; at large cohorts live checkoffs for 237 students caused queues and took about 80% of TA office-hour time, and one lockdown platform broke at 300 users [R95], [R89].

Staff time and cost: supervised tests need invigilation, venues and timetabling, and secure items need fresh question writing [R84], [R25]; no study reported venue or licence costs in money terms, so budgets must be estimated locally.

Policy: programme-level securing means choosing which assessments to secure and may require removing others, as one programme removed a first-year exam to fund secured code reviews [R68]; staff resistance and accreditation are named barriers [R04], [R68].

Equity: supervision removes unequal access to paid AI tools [S342], [S001], but over-reliance on in-class formats may disadvantage non-native speakers and students with disabilities, and lockdown browsers failed for about 2-3% of students [R51], [R25].
Security: online proctoring, lockdown browsers and interface restrictions are weaker variants and can be bypassed, so the protection described here applies to in-person invigilation [R25], [R77].
evidence_status_basis: Parts of the redesign were implemented and evaluated in computing courses (computing = Y in tested_redesigns.md): live checkoffs in real developer tools with scripted questions and rubrics, run with 237 students, with scores, surveys and queue logs reported [R95]; invigilated exam tasks correcting LLM-generated Java code, compared with instructor-designed tasks across terms [R33]; and a supervised live demo within the redesigned TAP framework for 60 students [R81]. A supervised closed-book lab exam inside a project framework was also reported in a partly computing course [R93]. The programme-level choice of which assessments to secure is guidance only [R68], [R04] and has not been tested as a redesign.
risks_and_limits: No study directly tested covert AI use under in-person invigilation, and the exam items themselves are highly AI-solvable, so any breach of supervision is high-impact [S009], [S008], [D03]. Question wording is not a security measure [J3]. Checkoff scores showed ceiling effects, so they confirm baseline proficiency rather than grade it [R95], and students scored lower on AI-correction tasks without prior training [R33]. The redesign does not by itself make supervised work authentic or develop responsible AI use; those depend on the paired AI-permitted tasks.
